The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

So, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](images/dd/dd733ebebc7131eb2762e6e98e1d14d07a730e5e37657c639ae9cc46be123ee2.svg)

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -5 & 7 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 13\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & 22 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 13\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}= & [\begin{aligned}\,4 & 22 \\ \,1 & 13\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-c8443228-62d0-53de-820f-4c2c2789eb2f" :question/id #uuid "c8443228-62d0-53de-820f-4c2c2789eb2f" :question/math-academy-id "q-113104" :question/problem "Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$

$$" :question/worked-solution "The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

"Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}.$ 
What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & =2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}, \\ {b}_{2} & =4{c}_{1}-2{c}_{3}, \\ {b}_{3} & =2{c}_{1}-3{c}_{3},\end{aligned}
$$

and  the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & a & 2 \\ b & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & c & -3\end{aligned}]?
$$" :question/worked-solution "The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=4,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4928869d-0a7f-5e17-a81c-6aaf1def0a0c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} Find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to S}$ from $B$ to $S$ if 

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors of $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\,\text{ and }\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 9\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -6 & 9\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-987253ee-4461-5046-b1db-ce4100ac59cc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

$$

"Let $B={[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}$  be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-6){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-08ec3541-b791-5354-9296-f775e0ff2635"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is 

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & a & 7 \\ -1 & 4 & b \\ 4 & c & -9\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5 \\ -9\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 8 & 7 \\ -1 & 4 & 5 \\ 4 & 7 & -9\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=8,$ $b=5,$ and $c=7.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8192819f-c781-5fbc-98ce-44030ec1bb27"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} $$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-6){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

In expanded form, the matrix looks as follows:
![](images/06/062187705e6074afa6b5356be64f8deb878be540e2c3b236b22dbd244b872cc6.svg)

For example, let's consider two bases $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ given by 

$$
\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2\}, \qquad\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2\}.

![](images/32/32409a45b5ebcf6b8c1cc43404126b514066ace8d8c71bcec2e99f759833ec84.svg) 

then the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by

$$

$$

$$
[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal C} = P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} \cdot [\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}.
$$

:question/problem "Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5 \\ -9\end{aligned}],
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is 

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & a & 7 \\ -1 & 4 & b \\ 4 & c & -9\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-9a2d831b-a3f1-5313-8aee-60f8e3a93edc" :question/worked-solution "Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5 \\ -9\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 8 & 7 \\ -1 & 4 & 5 \\ 4 & 7 & -9\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=8,$ $b=5,$ and $c=7.$"] ["question-9a2d831b-a3f1-5313-8aee-60f8e3a93edc" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-8192819f-c781-5fbc-98ce-44030ec1bb27" Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-6){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$

${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & -6 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$"] [17592186124916 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-249ce60b-00ae-5912-900c-fca2a8f69bfe" :answer-field/id #uuid "249ce60b-00ae-5912-900c-fca2a8f69bfe"] $$

$$

and  the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$

$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ 
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to S}$ from $B$ to $S$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors of $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

:question/problem "Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is 

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & a \\ b & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & c & 2\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=0,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-5.$"} {:db/id 17592186391991 :question/id #uuid "c0e29690-0559-5609-84c1-8e332dcb9ec7" :question/math-academy-id "q-36401"} {:db/id 17592186394291 :question/id #uuid ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 11 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}11 & -2 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186386689 :question/id #uuid "4593a4d9-b03b-5c1f-ad85-95d87fe0ce9e" :question/math-academy-id "q-113513"} {:db/id 17592186391984 :question/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Given two bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ of a vector space $V,$ the **change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$** is the matrix $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$.

In expanded form, the matrix looks as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ [{b}_{1}]_{C} & [{b}_{2}]_{C} & … & [{b}_{n}]_{C} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}
$$

For example, let's consider two bases $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ given by 

$$
\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2\}, \qquad\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2\}.
$$

If we happen to know that

$$
[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 11\end{aligned}]
$$

 

then the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}= & [\begin{aligned}-12 & 3 \\ 11 & 6\end{aligned}]. \\  & \,{↑}_{[{b}_{1}]_{C}}\,{↑}_{[{b}_{2}]_{C}}\end{aligned}
$$

The beauty of the change-of-coordinates matrix is that it allows us to express the vector $[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}$ in the basis $\mathcal C$ via the transformation

$$
[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal C} = P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} \cdot [\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}.
$$

This can be visualized as shown below.

$$
P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}

Recall that the columns of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C},$ that is

$$
\begin{aligned}| & | \\ [{b}_{1}]_{C} & [{b}_{2}]_{C} \\ | & |\end{aligned}
$$

To compute $P_{\small{\color{black}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{black}\mathcal{C}}},$ we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}= & [\begin{aligned}-12 & 3 \\ 11 & 6\end{aligned}]. \\  & \,{↑}_{[{b}_{1}]_{C}}\,{↑}_{[{b}_{2}]_{C}}\end{aligned}
$$

The beauty of the change-of-coordinates matrix is that it allows us to express the vector $[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}$ in the basis $\mathcal C$ via the transformation

$$
[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal C} = P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} \cdot [\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}.
$$

theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.
Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating
